data.title: ‘Not Out of the Woods,’ Says Top Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has had a mixed few weeks, and the stock has only listened to the bad half. Its third-quarter earnings report on Nov. 9 showed record sales and a wave of new contracts, and on Nov. 14 its small Electron rocket flew for the 100th time. But Neutron, the bigger rocket the company is counting on, won’t fly until 2027 after a delay announced in October, and losses are getting deeper. A short rally after the report faded within days, and the shares have since handed most of the gains back to the market. The stock now sits ~64% below its late-May peak.

Considering the company’s excellent growth profile, could investors have an opportunity to load up at a discount? A top investor using the moniker of The Asian Investor (TAI) went through the report to see whether that’s the case.

The investor gives Rocket Lab credit for the top line. Revenue jumped 73% year over year to a record $267.8 million, beating Wall Street’s forecast and the top of management’s own range. Backlog grew 52% from the prior quarter to about $3.6 billion. That’s split fairly evenly between launch services and Space Systems, the unit that builds satellites and spacecraft hardware. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of $270 million to $290 million, which would take full-year sales close to $1 billion, roughly 63% above 2025.

The bottom line is another matter. Rocket Lab lost $79.7 million in the quarter, more than four times its loss a year earlier and wider than analysts expected. TAI, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, blames heavier R&D and operating spending as the company builds Neutron, its medium-lift rocket, plus a $27.3 million loss on extinguishment of debt. Another $21.3 million went to transaction costs, mostly for the pending $8 billion purchase of satellite operator Iridium Communications.

The slide also hasn’t made the stock cheap. With a market cap of about $36 billion, Rocket Lab trades at roughly 40x trailing 12-month sales. Three other companies that rely heavily on government contracts are far cheaper. L3Harris trades at under 3x sales, Redwire at around 3x, and Intuitive Machines at around 3.5x. TAI thinks the market is pricing in a lot of growth, and much of it depends on a rocket that hasn’t flown yet.

Which brings us to Neutron, the deciding factor. On Oct. 14, Rocket Lab pushed the rocket’s debut into 2027 after finding flaws in a fuel tank component, and it hasn’t set a new date. TAI expects the first flight in the first half of next year. A clean launch would lift the mood around the stock and open up a new business carrying heavier payloads. Another slip would put even more attention on the losses.

“With management not providing enough clarity about when it will launch its medium-to-heavy-duty Neutron rocket and heavy losses weighing on Rocket Lab’s financial performance, I expect a weak investment setup at least for the next several months,” the 5-star investor summed up.

Accordingly, TAI rates Rocket Lab stock a Sell. (To watch The Asian Investor’s track record, click here)

However, none of the Street’s analysts agree with that take. In fact, based on a mix of 15 Buys and 3 Holds, the consensus view is that this stock is a Strong Buy. At $95.41, the average price target implies shares will gain 73% in the months ahead. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘No Respect,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) spent the first half of the year as one of the hottest names in the AI trade, but the tables have turned since then. Doubts over how long the memory boom can run, a chip selloff after the midterm elections and the leadership turmoil at Nvidia have all weighed on the memory giant.

Today, investors hoped Nvidia’s strong third-quarter results would spark a rebound, but that hasn’t happened, and the stock is down once again. The shares now sit about 43% below their record close in late June.

Yet, for those wondering if the stock will reclaim its June highs any time soon, investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to The Motley Fool, thinks the market has badly misjudged how long this upswing will last.

The investor accepts that memory has always moved in cycles of shortage and oversupply, and that the good times usually fade within a year or so. Drury argues this cycle has broken that pattern. AI data centers are taking every chip the industry can make, and Micron and its rivals have committed their output far into the future. Management backed that up at Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter report on Sept. 30, saying it expects supply to be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than it was in 2026, a year when memory was already scarce. More than 75% of Micron’s 2027 output is already spoken for.

In Drury’s view, that outlook should have reset the way investors value the stock. So far, the share price shows no sign of it. Micron trades at less than 5 times forward earnings, compared with about 18 times for the S&P 500, according to FactSet. The investor agrees that a cyclical company deserves to trade at a discount to the broader market, but considers this gap much too big. Even a multiple of about 10 times earnings, well below where Micron traded earlier this year, would be enough for the stock to more than double within a year or so, by Drury’s reckoning.

Looking further out, the investor is even more upbeat. Drury expects AI infrastructure spending to continue until at least 2030, which would keep Micron producing at full tilt and earning close to peak profits for years. The company also has several new plants due to open over the next few years. The investor expects customers to snap up that extra capacity as soon as it comes online, so it should add to growth rather than create a glut.

As for claiming June’s highs again, Drury thinks that hurdle will be overcome, and then  some. “I could see Micron’s stock tripling over the next three years as its valuation rises to a more respectable level and the market realizes that this cycle will last much longer,” Drury summed up. (To watch Drury’s track record, click here)

Almost all of the Street’s analysts agree with that take. Barring 1 Hold rating, all 28 other recent reviews are positive, making the consensus view a Strong Buy. At $1,624, the average price target factors in a 12-month returns of 135%. (See MU stock forecast)

data.title: Micron vs. Sandisk: Why Top Analyst Says Buy One AI Stock, Hold the Other
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) are extending their losses on Wednesday, falling between 3% and 4%, as Nvidia’s confirmation that former CEO Jensen Huang will not return weighs on sentiment throughout the semiconductor sector.

The recent selloff has been especially severe for investors who purchased shares near their highs. Micron has now fallen 36% from its October peak, although the stock remains up 145% year-to-date. Sandisk’s retreat has been even steeper, with shares plunging 65% from their June high while somehow still maintaining a 222% gain in 2026.

For RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri, who ranks among Wall Street’s top 2%, the recent weakness presents investors with an opportunity, but only in one of these stocks. The top analyst believes Micron deserves an Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating, while his stance on Sandisk is neither Buy nor Sell, leaving the stock with a Sector Perform (i.e., Hold) recommendation. (To watch Pajjuri’s track record, click here)

Micron: Why the Recent Selloff Could Be a Buying Opportunity

Pajjuri’s confidence in Micron strengthened following a recent investor meeting with company executives, where discussions focused on memory demand, technological developments, and long-term financial prospects.

The analyst came away convinced that investors are overlooking the company’s earnings potential, especially as AI applications require greater amounts of advanced memory.

“Overall, we walked away comfortable with our positive stance and view the recent pullback as an excellent opportunity,” Pajjuri wrote.

Pajjuri points out that manufacturing constraints, more complex production processes, and growing demand for high-bandwidth memory could keep industry supply tight over the next several years. These conditions may help prevent the oversupply that has historically hurt chipmakers, supporting stronger pricing and profitability.

Pajjuri also sees Micron benefiting from longer-term customer agreements, which offer greater predictability regarding future orders. Meanwhile, the company’s plans to distribute surplus funds through repurchases could provide additional support for its valuation.

Another reason for his confidence involves Micron’s technological capabilities, amid concerns that Chinese manufacturers could threaten its competitive position.

“We walked away comfortable with MU’s technology roadmap and product leadership and believe that recent concerns regarding China 4F² development are overdone,” the analyst commented.

Pajjuri believes Micron possesses the engineering capabilities necessary to defend its market position despite overseas competition. Its work on next-generation DRAM, advanced packaging, and sophisticated storage products could help preserve its advantages.

With shares trading at just 4.2 times his estimated calendar 2027 earnings, Pajjuri believes investors are paying too little for the company’s longer-term prospects. His Outperform rating on MU comes with a $1,500 price target, which implies about 114% upside from current levels. (See MU stock forecast)

Sandisk: Strong Results, but Valuation Concerns Remain

Pajjuri’s view of Sandisk is more reserved, despite the company’s encouraging financial performance and continued strength in NAND flash memory pricing.

The analyst acknowledges that demand from data centers remains healthy, supported by growing requirements for storage-intensive AI applications. Sandisk has also secured additional long-term customers, with about half its fiscal 2027 NAND bit volumes and two-thirds of fiscal 2028 already committed under supply arrangements.

However, those advantages aren’t enough to convince Pajjuri that investors should purchase shares at current levels.

“We believe risk/reward is fairly balanced as strong GenAI demand, tight supply, and solid cash returns are counterbalanced by moderating ASP growth and weak PC/smartphone markets,” Pajjuri explained.

His caution reflects concerns that Sandisk’s favorable operating conditions may not translate into the same earnings acceleration investors have come to expect. Slower increases in selling prices could limit future profitability, while sluggish consumer electronics sales threaten another important source of revenue.

data.title: ‘Ready for More Pain?’ Investor Asks About Strategy Stock
data.description:
These are rough days once again for Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shareholders. Bitcoin is hovering near a three-month low and has fallen below the price Strategy paid for its coins on average. Index provider MSCI is about to show the stock the door, and the common shares now trade below the company’s own preferred stock.

Strategy’s fall rally has all but evaporated, and the stockslipped under $100 on Tuesday. It was the first time the common had traded beneath its STRC preferred since mid-August. MSCI said on Nov. 11 that it will drop Strategy from its USA Index after the Nov. 30 close, which also takes it out of the World and ACWI benchmarks.

So, with the stock falling again today, and now down by 55% over the past year, should investors mull over getting some exposure here? Only if you’re ready for more pain, says an investor using the moniker Capital Minded (CM).

CM is a long-term bitcoin bull and thinks the index exit is the smaller worry. CM is more bothered by where Strategy’s money has been going. In the third quarter, the company raised $5.41 billion from common stock sales, but only $588.1 million of it, about 11%, bought bitcoin. Most of the rest was held as cash or spent supporting STRC, a preferred stock that pays a 12% annual dividend, after its price fell below the $100 par value. Strategy also sold 5,552 bitcoins during the quarter to help pay preferred dividends. The most recent weekly filing looks the same: of $244.7 million raised, $33.4 million went to bitcoin and $206.3 million went to STRC buybacks.

To CM, this means common shareholders are now paying for the preferred holders. Strategy’s BTC Yield, its own measure of bitcoin per share, stood at negative 3.7% for the year as of late October. Each share now carries less bitcoin than it did when the year began.

The bills keep growing. Preferred dividends reached $419.6 million in Q3, roughly three times the year-ago amount. The software business produced only $89.6 million of gross profit, on revenue that fell 3% year over year. CM gives Strategy credit for building a $4.75 billion dollar reserve. But that cash is set aside for dividends and interest. Between September 2027 and September 2028, holders could also hand back about $5.9 billion of convertible notes for cash. The first $1.01 billion of those notes converts at roughly $183 a share, far above today’s price. CM argues that covering both would cost common shareholders one way or another.

The investor does praise management for getting STRC back to its $100 par value on Nov. 4, after 165 days below it. That matters because Strategy only sells new STRC at $100 or above, and those sales raise money without creating more common shares. STRC has since dipped just under $100, though, so that door is closed again for now.

Index funds hold about 13 million MSTR shares, and CM sees their selling as a short-term hit. The bigger problem is that the stock only beats holding bitcoin when buyers pay a premium for it. Strategy has been the fourth-largest U.S. issuer of capital this year, and losing MSCI’s automatic buyers makes that premium harder to win back.

CM would rethink the call if bitcoin purchases start to outpace STRC buybacks, preferred sales restart at par, and bitcoin per share grows for two quarters in a row. Until then, Capital Minded would rather own bitcoin directly and rates Strategy stock a Sell. (To watch Capital Minded’s track record, click here)

Wall Street has no truck with that bearish call. With 12 Buys set against 1 Hold, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 132%, given the average price target clocks in at $217.92. (See MSTR stock forecast)

data.title: SK Hynix vs. Micron: One AI Stock Is Good, the Other Is Better, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Nvidia’s earnings reports are usually read as a verdict on the whole AI trade. Tuesday’s report also worked as a progress check on the companies that sell it memory. Alongside a third-quarter beat, Nvidia said its commitments to buy parts from suppliers jumped during the quarter, mostly because of multiyear deals to lock in memory. Few companies stand to gain more from that than SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU), two of the three makers of the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that sits inside Nvidia’s AI chips.

Nvidia put those commitments at $390 billion, up from $279 billion three months earlier. Both memory stocks jumped before the bell on Wednesday and have swung back and forth since the open, a sign of how nervous the market still is about the AI trade. Either way, both have a lot of ground to make up. Micron is still about 41% below its June high, and SK Hynix’s U.S.-listed shares are roughly 38% under their September peak.

Top investor Leo Sun, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, has been weighing which of the two is the better long-term AI holding.

The investor starts with what they share. DRAM, not NAND, brings in the bulk of sales at both companies, and both are counting on HBM, a high-density type of DRAM that feeds Nvidia’s data center GPUs, to power their near-term growth. SK Hynix, based in South Korea, trails only Samsung in DRAM, with Idaho-based Micron in third place.

Where they split, in Sun’s view, is timing. SK Hynix was the first to mass-produce HBM3 in 2022, and that head start made it Nvidia’s main supplier just as AI spending took off. It moved on to HBM3E in 2024 and HBM4 this year. Micron passed on HBM3 entirely, entered with HBM3E in 2024, and has also reached HBM4. Demand for its chips still runs ahead of what it can make. There is a knock-on effect, too. Every bit of factory space the two put toward HBM is space they can’t use for ordinary DRAM and NAND, which has left the rest of the memory market short of supply.

The growth on both sides is huge. SK Hynix grew revenue 47% year over year in 2025 and more than doubled its net income. Analysts expect its 2026 revenue to nearly quadruple, then climb another 60% in 2027. Micron’s fiscal 2026, which ended in early September, was even wilder. Revenue climbed to $133.2 billion from $37.4 billion, gross margin rose to 80.7% from 39.8%, and net income jumped from about $8.5 billion to roughly $85 billion. Analysts see Micron’s sales roughly doubling again in fiscal 2027 before YoY growth drops to around 16% in fiscal 2028.

Sun sees that expected slowdown as the reason investors still value the pair like boom-and-bust chip stocks instead of paying up for AI growth. SK Hynix’s U.S.-listed shares trade at about 3 times forward earnings, and Micron at around 4.5 times. The investor also points to pressures from outside the industry. Inflation and high interest rates could cool AI spending and leave smaller neocloud companies struggling to build out. And the Democrats’ midterm wins earlier this month put new governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, three big data center states, who campaigned on tougher rules for data center construction.

None of that changes the long-term picture much for Sun. Both stocks are “growing like weeds,” but Sun ultimately comes down in favor of one over the other. “If I had to pick one over the other, I’d stick with SK Hynix instead of Micron for three simple reasons: it’s larger, it’s growing faster, and it will remain the market leader in HBM chips,” the 5-star investor summed up. (To watch Sun’s track record, click here)

The Street sees no reason to pick between the pair, rating both as Strong Buys. SKHY’s average price target lands at $268.50, a figure pointing to 12-month upside of 118%. MU is expected to gain 127%, considering its average target clocks in at $1,624. (See SKHY stock forecast or MU stock forecast)

data.title: AMAT, KLAC, LRCX, ASML: Bernstein Picks 4 Chip Stocks for the Global Semiconductor Spending Boom
data.description:
Bernstein has named Applied Materials (AMAT), KLA Corporation (KLAC), Lam Research (LRCX), and ASML (ASML) as its preferred semiconductor equipment stocks. The brokerage sees rising investment in advanced chip production and memory manufacturing supporting industry growth through 2028.

Bernstein has raised its global wafer fabrication equipment (WFE) spending forecast to $217 billion in 2027, up 39% year over year. It expects spending to rise another 28% to $279 billion in 2028.

The brokerage also said fears of earnings cuts across the sector may be overstated. Much of the investment planned for 2027 is already in place, while spending plans for 2028 also look firm.

Applied Materials: Top U.S. Pick

Applied Materials is Bernstein’s preferred U.S. semiconductor equipment stock. Analyst Stacy Rasgon reiterated his Buy rating and a $600 price target, implying 71.8% upside.

Bernstein expects Applied Materials to benefit from higher demand for chip-making tools, memory chips, and advanced chips. Growing demand for chip packaging and its expanding services business could provide further support. The brokerage also considers the stock relatively cheap compared with its peers.

KLA: Strong Market Position

Bernstein analyst David Dai reiterated his Buy rating on KLAC, while cutting his price target from $250 to $225 (55.6% upside).

The brokerage pointed to KLA’s strong market position and long-term growth potential. It also sees the company as less exposed to the risk of Chinese equipment replacement. Easier year-on-year comparisons and fewer supply limits could support stronger results for KLAC in 2027.

Lam Research: Gains from New Chip Technology

Rasgon maintained his Buy rating and $350 price target, implying 66.1% upside. The firm sees growth coming from new gate-all-around (GAA) chip designs, advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and NAND upgrades. Bernstein also cited the company’s strong execution and margins as reasons for being bullish on the stock.

ASML: Bernstein’s Top European Pick

ASML is Bernstein’s top pick among European semiconductor stocks. Rasgon has a Buy rating and a €2,500 price target, which implies 102.1% upside.

The brokerage forecasts ASML’s dollar-based revenue to grow at a 34% compound annual rate from 2025 to 2028. Higher spending on DRAM and advanced logic is expected to drive demand for ASML’s lithography tools. The brokerage also projects EUV revenue to grow at a 44% annual rate.

Which Semiconductor Stock Do Analysts Prefer?

According to TipRanks’ Stock Comparison Tool, all four companies carry a Strong Buy consensus rating.

However, ASML has the highest implied upside at 82.1%, followed by LRCX at 80.8%, AMAT at 63.9%, and KLAC at 54.6%.

data.title: Nvidia’s (NVDA) Post-Huang Era Looks Brighter than Its Stock Suggests
data.description:
Nvidia’s (NVDA) post-Huang era may look brighter than its stock price suggests, as Q3 results point to an artificial intelligence (AI) boom far from over. Before reporting its fiscal third-quarter results on November 17, the stock had fallen 35% from its October high, marking its steepest drawdown in roughly 19 months. Jensen Huang’s sudden departure and doubts about the massive investments in AI infrastructure had left the market on edge.

However, the results released after the market closed told a different story. Nvidia’s revenue more than doubled year-over-year, while strong guidance beat estimates. Even so, the technology giant is trading at just around 9x projected Fiscal 2028 earnings.

The market seems to believe Nvidia’s best days are behind it. I don’t buy that narrative. Instead, I’d rate NVDA a Buy. Buying low and selling high seems simple in theory, and Nvidia may be offering one of the best opportunities in recent memory to put that idea into practice.

Nvidia’s Growth Is Starting to Defy Logic

Something about Nvidia’s latest quarter feels almost absurd, with growth starting to defy logic. At a massive scale where most companies struggle to maintain double-digit growth, Nvidia just delivered 103% year-over-year revenue growth, reaching $115.8 billion in Q3. That’s almost $20 billion more than the previous quarter alone.

Even more impressive, Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, growing 110% year-over-year. Meanwhile, adjusted operating income surged 116% to nearly $78 billion. So there’s really no sign that Nvidia is sacrificing profitability to sustain this extraordinary growth.

What caught my attention the most was the guidance. Management expects approximately $130 billion in Q4 revenue — about 4% above market expectations — followed by an ambitious outlook for 75% revenue growth in Fiscal 2028.

The One Crack in an Otherwise Strong Quarter

Perhaps the most concerning detail was that, even though Q4 includes an extra week, gross margin is expected to decline to 71%–72%, down from 74.8% in Q3.

Yet this wasn’t new. Nvidia had already warned about this decline in August, mainly due to higher memory prices and the ramp-up of Vera Rubin — the company’s latest AI supercomputing platform.

Even with lower margins, gross profit should continue growing. Based on the midpoint of Q4 guidance, Nvidia could generate roughly $93 billion in gross profit, compared with about $87 billion in Q3. That’s an additional $6.2 billion, or roughly 7% growth, despite a 340-basis-point decline in gross margin.

Nvidia Is Doing More than Selling the Shovels

If Nvidia has been the biggest seller of “shovels” in the AI “gold rush,” it may now be doing much more than that. One of the more interesting details in Nvidia’s earnings report was where demand actually came from. So let’s follow the money.

Hyperscalers accounted for $60.1 billion in Data Center revenue, up from $48.7 billion in the previous quarter. That’s important because it suggests that the expansion of AI infrastructure isn’t being driven exclusively by speculative, externally financed startups. In fact, concerns about this, along with Jensen Huang’s departure, had recently become one of the main risks surrounding the NVDA bull case.

Meanwhile, Vera Rubin is already experiencing the fastest product ramp in Nvidia’s history, reinforcing the company’s technological moat. Of course, Nvidia was already selling integrated systems with Blackwell, but Vera Rubin takes this a step further. It combines central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), high-speed networking, and software into a single platform designed to deliver more computing power at lower energy costs.

That’s particularly important because competing with Nvidia isn’t simply a matter of developing a better or cheaper GPU. AMD (AMD), Broadcom (AVGO), and hyperscalers developing their own chips also need to challenge the efficiency of Nvidia’s entire ecosystem. That’s a much harder task.

Yet selling the shovels is one thing, and helping finance the gold rush is another. Nvidia now has approximately $518 billion in future commitments, mostly related to securing components and production capacity, alongside $118 billion in contingent financial guarantees. These aren’t immediate liabilities, but they illustrate just how deeply the company has become financially involved in building the AI ecosystem. To me, this remains arguably one of the biggest Achilles’ heels of Nvidia’s bull case.

The Post-Huang Discount Looks Hard to Justify

Perhaps after the impressive Q3 earnings, market attention has shifted away from hardware profit margins. Investors now focus entirely on a different question: can Nvidia sustain its trajectory without its founder and long-time CEO, Jensen Huang?

That’s a legitimate concern. Still, the latest quarter suggests its technological roadmap, customer relationships, execution capabilities, and operational scale remain intact.

Despite all this growth, Nvidia is trading at just 9x projected Fiscal 2028 earnings. That’s a surprisingly low multiple for a company still growing at this pace.

Based on current consensus estimates of around $16.23 in adjusted earnings per share (EPS) for FY2028, I believe a relatively modest 16x earnings multiple is reasonable, assuming Nvidia can maintain its current position in the AI market. That gives me a price target of approximately $260, implying nearly 67% upside from the stock’s current price.

Interestingly, that’s roughly the multiple investors are already paying for FY2027 earnings. In other words, my bullish scenario doesn’t require Nvidia to return to its historically elevated valuations. Much of the upside could come from earnings growth alone.

Nvidia’s Sell-Off Could Be Its Own Best Opportunity

There’s a certain irony in Nvidia’s recent sell-off. While bears question the sustainability of its revenue growth and whether it can maintain such high margins, Nvidia itself has an opportunity to buy back its shares at valuations that seemed almost unthinkable just a few months ago.

It certainly has the firepower to do so. Nvidia ended Q3 with $227.3 billion remaining under its repurchase authorization, while generating nearly $44 billion in quarterly free cash flow. At current share prices, fully using that authorization could retire roughly 6% of its outstanding shares. That could boost EPS by approximately 6.5%, even without any additional net income growth. That’s a meaningful tailwind for a company already expected to deliver extraordinary earnings growth.

So, in a way, the same sell-off that has frustrated shareholders also makes every dollar spent on buybacks potentially more accretive. At a time when even cash-rich hyperscalers like Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are increasingly turning to external financing to fund their AI ambitions, Nvidia is in a rather privileged position. It’s generating enough free cash flow to fund massive shareholder returns without having to rely on external financing to do so.

Is NVDA a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Yes, Wall Street analysts still see Nvidia as a Buy, although enthusiasm has cooled somewhat. The stock now carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating. Of the 42 analyst ratings issued over the past three months, 28 are Buys, 13 are Holds, and just one is a Sell. Still, the average Nvidia price target stands at $227.74, implying a solid 46.49% upside from current levels.

Nvidia’s Numbers Tell a Different Story

Nvidia’s Q3 results showed that the concerns weighing on its stock have yet to translate into weaker business performance. Hyperscaler demand remains exceptionally strong, and the company’s technological roadmap is moving forward despite Huang’s departure. More importantly, Nvidia is still delivering extraordinary earnings growth while trading at a multiple that suggests the opposite. That’s a disconnect worth taking advantage of. I remain Bullish on NVDA.

data.title: 3 High-Valuation Stocks with Strong Buy Ratings
data.description:
Using the TipRanks Stock Screener tool, we identified three high P/E stocks with Strong Buy consensus ratings and average analyst price targets implying at least 29% upside. Despite their premium valuations, analysts see further growth potential driven by AI demand and company-specific catalysts.

Why Do Some Stocks Have High P/E Ratios?

A high price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio does not necessarily mean a stock is overvalued. Some investors are willing to pay a premium for companies expected to deliver solid earnings growth. Strong industry trends and competitive advantages can also justify higher valuations. However, investors must assess whether future growth can support the current valuation.

Synopsys (SNPS)

  • P/E Ratio: 77.46x 
  • Average Synopsys Price Target: $587.76 (35% upside)

Synopsys provides electronic design automation (EDA) software, which is used to design and test semiconductor chips before they are manufactured. Synopsys operates in the highly specialized EDA market, where Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) is its closest competitor. Its competitive positioning, high switching costs, recurring revenue, and growing demand for advanced chip-design tools support its high valuation.

Synopsys is scheduled to release its Q4 FY26 results on December 8. Wall Street expects Synopsys to report earnings of $4.12 per share, up from $2.90 per share in the year-ago period. Revenue is projected to surge 13.8% year-over-year to $2.56 billion.

Block (XYZ)

  • P/E Ratio: 108.53x 
  • Average Block Price Target: $104.37 (31.6% upside)

Block is a fintech company that provides payment services for businesses through Square and financial services to consumers through Cash App. It also owns the buy now, pay later (BNPL) platform Afterpay.

Block surpassed both earnings and revenue estimates for Q3 FY26. Adjusted EPS came in at $1.13, versus analyst expectations of $1.03. Revenue increased 9.9% year-over-year to $6.72 billion, surpassing estimates of $6.59 billion. Growth was supported by strong performance across Cash App and Square, with Cash App gross profit rising 27% to $2.07 billion, driven partly by higher lending activity, while Square gross profit increased 14% to $1.16 billion.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)

  • P/E Ratio: 107.77x 
  • Average AMD Price Target: $652.18 (29.6% upside)

AMD designs high-performance chips that power computers, gaming consoles, and AI data centers. AMD is one of Nvidia’s (NVDA) biggest competitors in the rapidly growing AI chip market, while also gaining market share in server processors.

AMD beat Wall Street estimates in Q3 2026, reporting revenue of $13.38 billion, up 44.7% year-over-year, versus analyst expectations of $13.10 billion. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.09, beating consensus estimates of $1.95. Its Data Center revenue also grew 97% year-over-year in Q3 2026. With rising AI infrastructure spending, growing adoption of its EPYC server processors, and increasing demand for Instinct AI GPUs, AMD could capture a larger share of the AI computing market.

data.title: Goldman Sachs Pounds the Table on These 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks
data.description:
Strong corporate earnings have helped drive stock market gains throughout 2026, but investors are now looking ahead to what 2027 might bring. With concerns surrounding AI spending, elevated valuations, and the outlook for economic growth, Wall Street is weighing whether the bull market has enough room to continue.

Goldman Sachs strategist Peter Oppenheimer believes stocks can deliver further gains next year, although investors should prepare for a less favorable environment. The strategist expects earnings growth to moderate, borrowing costs to remain elevated, and market volatility to increase. Still, he sees reasons for confidence, arguing that continued economic expansion and opportunities beyond the AI sector should support equities.

“Equity markets typically rise so long as nominal GDP is growing, valuations are not excessive, and interest rates are not rising sharply. Nevertheless, the momentum of growth matters. The shift lower in equity markets in recent weeks – centred around AI concerns – has rapidly priced in the prospect of weaker growth rates, and the sharp sector and factor rotations within equities have pushed up the valuation of Defensive and Value parts of the market. From here, we expect equities to generate positive returns, albeit with higher volatility than in recent years. We expect investors to seek companies that can sustain growth as it becomes more scarce,” Oppenheimer wrote.

Against this backdrop, Goldman Sachs analysts have singled out two stocks they believe offer compelling opportunities heading into 2027. According to TipRanks database, both also carry Strong Buy consensus ratings and offer double-digit upside potential based on Wall Street’s average price targets. Let’s take a closer look at what makes these two names worth considering.

Accelevation Holdings (ACCV)

AI might be slowing down, but it remains a powerful growth driver – and Accelevation caters directly to the AI economy. The company serves the mega-cap tech firms – companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle – that have been defining the AI revolution. Specifically, Accelevation designs, manufactures, and installs the structural, electrical, and mechanical systems that form the mission-critical infrastructure that turns massive empty buildings into data centers.

Accelevation’s product lines include vital components to integrate liquid cooling piping, airflow containment, power distribution, and structural/rack-level conveyance into the building structures. In addition, Accelevation provides interior steel structures and conveyance systems, along with high-density remote power panels (RPPs), power distribution units (PDUs), and branch circuit whips, all vital in distributing the high-power loads required to keep a data center running.

The company is based in Ohio, where it has its corporate headquarters, along with manufacturing facilities for a wide range of products. The company also has facilities in Virginia, Texas, Georgia, Arizona, Mississippi, and Tennessee. This network of facilities allows Accelevation to offer its customers a secure product source that supports American manufacturing.

Accelevation went public at the end of September, through an IPO that saw the ticker start trading on the last day of the month. The IPO included a total of 30,000,000 shares, set at a price of $18; the gross proceeds came to $540 million. Of that total, Accelevation raised $180 million in gross proceeds from the 10,000,000 shares it sold directly, receiving ~$170.6 million after offering expenses. The other 20,000,000 shares were sold by existing shareholders affiliated with Olympus Partners.

While a new company in the public markets, Accelevation has already released a quarterly financial report. That release, for 3Q26, showed revenues of $202.2 million, up 65.9% year-over-year and $9.34 million over the estimates. The company’s forward outlook is strong – bookings in Q3 were up 364% year-over-year to reach $768.9 million, and the work backlog of $1.7 billion marked a 329% y/y jump.

Accelevation falls under the coverage purview of 5-star Goldman analyst Joe Ritchie, who believes that the company’s essential services to the largest players in the AI universe give it a leg up going forward.

“While the broader data center gray space market is more crowded and competitive, ACCV has carved out a high-value niche within the data center white space. With one of the few platforms capable of executing end-to-end solutions (from platform design to domestic manufacturing to self-performed installation), ACCV reduces traditional deployment timelines. As a result, ACCV serves as a critical last-mile partner for the world’s largest hyperscalers racing to expand capacity. By acting as the basis-of-design for at least three major hyperscalers, ACCV embeds its engineering teams at the genesis of a project to translate severe spatial and thermal constraints into scalable solutions. This early engagement creates customer stickiness and repeat deployments across mega-campuses,” Ritchie noted.

“We believe ACCV’s focus on factory-built modularity also limits field labor constraints and minimizes multi-vendor interface risk, which is an additional value add for their customers. We expect ACCV to be the fastest-growing company in our coverage over the next three years (+74%) compounding EBITDA 77% over that time frame,” the analyst added.

Ritchie goes on to give ACCV shares a Buy rating with a $22 price target to indicate room for a 12-month upside of 109%. (To watch Ritchie’s track record, click here)

There are currently 8 recent analyst reviews on this stock, with a 7 to 1 split that supports a Strong Buy consensus rating. ACCV is selling for $10.51 and its $19.33 average price target implies that it will appreciate by 84% on the one-year horizon. (See ACCV stock forecast)

HawkEye 360 (HAWK)

The next Goldman Sachs pick to look at here is HawkEye 360, a tech company focusing on signals intelligence and data analytics. HawkEye 360 lives at the cutting edge of this field, working in the defense and intelligence sectors where it provides a range of services, including spectrum monitoring of radar, communications, and navigation signal systems; maritime intelligence, including commercial and military vessel tracking, and ‘dark vessel’ identification; GNSS interference detection, to locate GPS jamming and/or spoofing; and air defense and communications and radar systems monitoring.

That’s a serious list of capabilities, and one in high demand by governments and militaries. HawkEye 360’s ability to detect and analyze radio-frequency emissions worldwide makes the company a valuable intelligence partner for governments and militaries seeking greater visibility into potential security threats.

Like many companies of its ilk, HawkEye 360 is based in the environs of Washington DC. The company’s HQ is in Herndon, Virginia, right between DC and Dulles Airport, and not far from the Pentagon, giving the firm ready access to the full array of US government and military agencies, as well as federal and state law enforcement agencies. The company has also made moves in recent years to expand – in 2025, it acquired the Texas-based Innovative Signal Analysis, ISA, a firm that develops signals intelligence (SIGINT) and image-processing tech for the US government, military branches, intelligence services, and homeland security agencies. The acquisition was supported by $150 million in equity and debt financing.

HawkEye 360 is relatively new to the public markets, having held its IPO in May of this year. The company raised $478.4 million in gross proceeds through its IPO, selling 18.4 million shares, including those purchased through the underwriters’ option. We should note that, since the IPO, shares in HAWK are down more than 46%, although the stock bottomed out in October and is up some 47% in the past 30 days.

On the financial side, HawkEye 360 reported several solid metrics in its last quarterly report, covering 3Q26. The top-line revenue figure of $59.3 million was up 84% year-over-year and beat the forecast by nearly $3 million. Of that total, $23.3 million was international revenue – a company record and a 76% increase from the prior year. HawkEye 360 also reported a work backlog of $300.3 million and bumped up its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to the range of $225 million to $227 million.

For Goldman analyst Noah Poponak, the fact of an unstable geopolitical situation provides a clear foundation for HAWK shares to rest on.

“International momentum remains strong, as geopolitical conflicts and the national security agendas of U.S. allies and partners drives the adoption of HAWK’s products and services. The recent ISA acquisition is a bright spot as well, contributing more revenue than our model expected, and providing additional signals processing capabilities that help drive additional HAWK customer penetration and sales. HAWK successfully deployed Block II Clusters 15 and 16 in October, and has secured launch supply through 2028. We continue to think HAWK occupies a unique space within the broader defense and signals intelligence ecosystem with a profitable business model,” Poponak noted.

The Goldman analyst rates HAWK as a Buy, and his price target, set at $32, implies a 12-month gain of 73%. (To watch Poponak’s track record, click here)

Overall, all 7 of the recent analyst reviews of HAWK are positive, making the Strong Buy consensus rating unanimous. The stock is currently priced at $18.45 and has a $25.29 average target price, suggesting a 37% upside by this time next year. (See HAWK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘It’s Still a Strong Sell,’ Says Investor on Nvidia Stock After Earnings
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is keeping Wall Street on its toes, with shares edging 1% higher in overnight trading after jumping as much as 5.5% following Tuesday’s fiscal third-quarter earnings release. The AI chip leader delivered results that exceeded expectations and offered an upbeat financial outlook, giving investors reason to feel encouraged despite the uncertainty surrounding Jensen Huang’s high-profile departure.

The numbers certainly provided reassurance, with revenue soaring 103% year-over-year to $115.84 billion and adjusted earnings reaching $2.68 per share, beating analysts’ estimates on both counts. Better yet, interim CEO Colette Kress projected fourth-quarter sales of $130 billion, above the consensus forecast of $125.3 billion. However, Tuesday’s conference call also confirmed that the board has no plans to reinstate Huang, leaving the semiconductor powerhouse facing an uncertain future without its longtime founder.

Against this backdrop, investor Louis Liu maintains that NVDA shares still deserve a Strong Sell rating, arguing that the market has underestimated several threats capable of undermining the company’s long-term prospects.

His skepticism begins with Nvidia’s commanding position in AI computing, which he believes will become harder to defend as competitors gain ground.

“The gap is just too large to be sustainable in a competitive race, especially given that leadership in semiconductors rarely stays fixed for as long as people expect,” Liu explained.

His reasoning suggests that Nvidia’s premium valuation depends on preserving its technological advantages, while rivals can reward investors simply by capturing additional demand. That leaves Nvidia vulnerable if customers gradually diversify their suppliers or develop proprietary processors.

However, Liu considers Huang’s departure an even more immediate concern, given the former chief executive’s central role in developing Nvidia’s technological strategy and competitive strengths. Although existing products and customer relationships remain intact, the investor believes replacing such an influential founder presents a formidable challenge.

“To the extent the stock carried a premium for the continuation of that leadership, his departure gives investors reason to pause,” Liu wrote.

The investor worries that future decisions involving chip development, strategic partnerships, and acquisitions could suffer without Huang’s engineering expertise. While Kress brings extensive financial experience, her ability to guide the organization’s technical direction remains unproven.

Beyond the leadership transition, Liu sees another serious threat developing in Washington, where scrutiny of advanced semiconductor shipments through Southeast Asia could eventually lead to tighter export restrictions or financial penalties.

“What if the U.S. federal government imposes a huge fine upon Nvidia,” Liu asked, raising concerns about potential consequences from alleged violations of export regulations.

Such an outcome could hurt profitability while making the stock’s elevated valuation harder to justify, especially if competitors capitalize on any disruption. These regulatory risks remain hypothetical, although Liu believes their possible financial impact deserves greater consideration.

And while Tuesday’s strong earnings challenged his pessimistic outlook, the latest figures haven’t persuaded Liu to reconsider his position. He acknowledges that the quarterly performance strengthens the bullish argument, but maintains that near-term success cannot resolve longer-term uncertainties involving competition, executive succession, and government intervention. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has just passed its first big test without Jensen Huang, sending shares about 4.5% higher in overnight trading following strong fiscal third-quarter results. The earnings release and subsequent conference call offered investors their first glimpse of how the AI chip leader intends to navigate life after its longtime CEO, whose abrupt removal stunned Wall Street.

And the numbers certainly gave investors reason to feel encouraged, with revenue soaring 103% year-over-year to $115.84 billion and adjusted earnings reaching $2.68 per share, beating expectations on both counts. Better yet, the company projected fourth-quarter sales of $130 billion, above analysts’ $125.2 billion estimate.

That confidence is precisely what caught the eye of top analyst Daniel Ives, who ranks among the top 4% of Wall Street experts. While Tuesday’s financial results were encouraging, Ives believes Kress’s willingness to deliver such an upbeat forecast during her first earnings call as interim chief executive deserves serious consideration, given the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s leadership transition.

“The guide is the most important line in the release,” Ives wrote.

The analyst sees this decision as evidence of considerable financial visibility, suggesting Nvidia has enough customer commitments to support aggressive growth projections despite the executive shakeup. The outlook also excludes Chinese data center computing sales, making the company’s confidence in future performance all the more compelling.

Looking further ahead, Kress raised Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 year-over-year revenue growth outlook to 75% from 70%, reflecting expectations for continued expansion. Meanwhile, cloud industry backlog has reached $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months earlier, pointing to sustained spending on AI infrastructure.

However, while Nvidia’s financial performance appears to have eased immediate concerns about its future, the leadership crisis remains far from over, according to Ives.

“A clean quarter and guide strengthen the board’s hand but do not close the question,” the analyst cautioned.

The remaining obstacles involve potential intervention by activist investors, the possibility of a special shareholder meeting, and the ongoing U.S. investigation into advanced chip exports. Those developments could determine whether Nvidia’s directors successfully navigate the current turmoil or face further challenges to their authority.

Meanwhile, the company has already ruled out bringing Huang back, retaining Heidrick & Struggles to oversee the search for a permanent successor. Directors have also established a dedicated national security and export compliance committee, although the circumstances surrounding the former CEO’s departure remain undisclosed.

Despite these uncertainties, Ives remains bullish on Nvidia’s prospects, maintaining his Outperform rating and $225 price target, which implies about 45% upside from Tuesday’s closing price. (To watch Ives’ track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Don’t Gamble,’ Says Wall Street’s Biggest Bear on Nvidia Stock Before Earnings
data.description:
The moment of truth has arrived for Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), with the AI chip giant about to release its fiscal third-quarter earnings after the closing bell. Shares are slipping another 1.8% ahead of the announcement, extending a miserable run that has wiped out 36% of their value since October’s high. Investors are now wondering whether tonight’s results can stop the bleeding or send the stock tumbling further.

The stakes could hardly be higher following Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure, which has left CFO Colette Kress steering Nvidia through one of its most turbulent periods in years. Washington’s growing scrutiny of advanced chip exports to China threatens another blow, while mounting fears about the financial stability of smaller cloud customers have raised doubts about future revenue. With confidence already badly shaken, even blockbuster earnings might fail to rescue the battered stock unless Nvidia delivers convincing evidence that its growth story remains intact.

And Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg, Wall Street’s biggest Nvidia bear, believes those hoping for an earnings-driven comeback could be headed for another disappointment.

“Unfortunately, we think the company’s struggles are going to get worse and there may be another leg down for the stock,” Goldberg warned.

Ahead of the print, the analyst assigns NVDA shares a Sell rating, while slashing his price target from $180 to $130, implying about 16% downside from current levels. (To watch Goldberg’s track record, click here)

One of Goldberg’s biggest worries involves Nvidia’s exposure to Asian markets, where questions surrounding the ultimate destinations of advanced processors could invite tougher regulatory action. The analyst points to uncertainty surrounding shipments routed through Malaysia, Singapore, and Taiwan, arguing that the company needs to provide greater transparency regarding its customers and distribution channels.

The analyst also doubts Nvidia can continue dictating terms to its largest tech customers as confidently as it did under Huang. Companies operating massive data centers could use the leadership transition to negotiate more favorable purchasing arrangements, potentially squeezing profitability even if overall demand remains healthy.

Another concern revolves around the smaller cloud operators that have become more important to Nvidia’s financial performance. Goldberg estimates that these so-called neoclouds account for about 40% of revenue, making their dependence on continued financial support a potentially serious vulnerability. The analyst expects Nvidia to reduce the scale of its backing for these operators, which could weaken an important source of orders while leaving the company more dependent on lower-margin sales to tech giants.

Goldberg is equally worried about the relationships that helped Nvidia dominate the semiconductor industry over the past several years. Asian suppliers appear hesitant to make long-term commitments until a permanent chief executive takes charge, raising concerns about how smoothly the company’s operations can continue.

Employee retention presents another potential obstacle, with Huang’s removal threatening the loyalty that previously helped Nvidia keep valuable engineering talent within the organization.

“We think there is real risk Nvidia starts to see more significant levels of employee attrition,” Goldberg cautioned.

Ultimately, Goldberg believes Nvidia’s existing order backlog could sustain operations through the next few quarters, but restoring confidence may require far more than another blockbuster earnings announcement. For investors considering buying the dip, his message is clear: the risks may still outweigh the potential rewards. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: Lock In the Consumer Staples Sector with This ETF
data.description:
Monday was another rough day for the major indexes. On the other hand, it was a pretty good day for the consumer staples sector. 

Consider that the S&P 500 is now up 8.7% for the year. Meanwhile, the State Street Consumer Select Staples ETF (XLP) has gained over 19% year-to-date. Over the past month, XLP has gained 5.87%, while the S&P 500 has fallen by 2.6%. 

XLP, which is a bellwether for the consumer staples sector, closed at an all-time high on Monday:

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 last reached an all-time closing high over a month ago, on October 6.

The S&P 500 is now less than 100 points away from its 200-day moving average (red), currently located at 7342. Just beneath it, near 7300, is a trend line that has been intact since April 2025 (black dotted line).

Nasdaq Correction 

The Nasdaq Composite also last reached an all-time high on October 6, and has since fallen into correction territory, losing nearly 11%. For the major indexes, a decline of greater than 10% from the highs is considered a correction. 

We’ve been selling tech and buying staples for some time now. In recent weeks, we’ve featured J.M. Smucker (SJM), McDonald’s (MCD), Walmart (WMT), and Merck (MRK). We did this while exiting the semiconductor sector. 

If you’re late to the party, or if you’re just looking to add a diversified group of staples stocks to your portfolio with one click, I’d recommend the aforementioned State Street Consumer Select Staples ETF (XLP). 

What’s in XLP?

Here’s a recent breakdown of XLP’s top holdings:

  • Walmart 11.24%
  • Costco Wholesale (COST) 9.6%
  • Procter & Gamble (PG) 7.7%
  • Coca-Cola (KO) 7.6%
  • Phillip Morris (PM) 6.1%
  • Altria Group (MO) 4.6%
  • Colgate-Palmolive (CL) 4.5%
  • Mondelez International (MDLZ) 4.3%
  • PepsiCo (PEP) 4.2%
  • Target (TGT) 4.1%

What’s the Downside?

In recent years, tech selloffs have been temporary. When those selloffs did occur, consumer staples stocks took off, only to fall back to earth as tech came roaring back. 

While that could happen again, this time does seem different. We’ve just seen Nvidia (NVDA), the darling of the market with a 371% return over the past five years, lose 35% since October 6. That stock is technically damaged, closing at a 52-week low on Monday.

With the price falling below the $165 support level (arrow), Nvidia could see a further decline. Earnings are expected after Tuesday’s close. 

Broader Tech Selling

Although Nvidia’s problems are unique to that company, we’re seeing an across-the-board selloff in semiconductors specifically, and in tech in general.

Since October 6, Micron (MU) is down 30%. Micron is trading below its 200-day moving average (red), and its 50-day moving average (blue) is curling downward.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) (right chart) is in better shape than Micron, but has lost 22% since October 6.

Sandisk (SNDK) has declined an incredible 65% since June.

Bottom Line

While consumer staples aren’t guaranteed to outperform the markets, they are a steady alternative to volatile tech stocks. These are not the most exciting companies, but they make real products and have real earnings. The State Street Consumer Select Staples ETF provides a solid roster of names in this sector.

data.title: Buy Micron Stock Before the Company Does, Says Investor
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock is falling for a fourth consecutive trading session on Tuesday, losing about 2.5% as the AI memory chipmaker struggles to find its footing. Shares have now plunged 37% from their early October peak, erasing a large portion of the gains accumulated during this year’s rally. Despite soaring demand for advanced semiconductors, investors are growing nervous about the industry’s near-term prospects.

Much of the uncertainty stems from the fallout surrounding Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, alongside growing calls for tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chip exports. Meanwhile, Democrats have launched investigations into the Trump administration’s handling of semiconductor sales to China, raising fears of additional regulatory hurdles for the industry. Adding to Micron’s troubles, a class-action lawsuit accusing leading memory manufacturers of conspiring to manipulate DRAM prices has raised further concerns.

Yet, investor Adam Spatacco, who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes the recent selloff presents an opportunity worth considering ahead of December. His bullish outlook revolves around an approaching change in Micron’s ability to repurchase its own shares, potentially allowing the company to capitalize on its battered valuation.

“To me, Micron’s expanded buyback program gives investors a new reason to consider buying the stock before Dec. 9,” Spatacco wrote.

The date matters due to restrictions associated with federal CHIPS Act funding agreements, which have limited corporate purchases of outstanding equity during the past two years. Those limitations are scheduled to change on December 9, giving Micron greater flexibility to repurchase shares, although future transactions will remain subject to financial conditions under its CHIPS Act agreements.

The financial implications could be significant, especially considering how little money the company has devoted to these transactions recently. During fiscal 2026, Micron acquired just 2.5 million shares for $650 million, following an earlier annual period without any repurchases whatsoever. However, its board expanded the existing authorization to $35.16 billion on October 8, providing ample capacity for future activity.

Spatacco also sees another advantage created by the recent collapse in the stock’s valuation. Using a hypothetical $10 billion expenditure, the investor calculates that Micron could have purchased 9.4 million shares at September 30 prices, compared with 13.6 million at November 16 levels. That represents nearly 45% more equity retired without spending an additional dollar.

Such transactions would reduce the total number of outstanding shares, potentially lifting earnings per share even without corresponding improvements in overall profitability. Combined with growing demand for sophisticated memory components in AI data centers, this could strengthen the investment case as the semiconductor industry navigates its current uncertainty.

“For investors with a long-term time horizon who can stomach some short-term volatility in the semiconductor industry, buying Micron stock before the repurchase program becomes available could prove more rewarding than waiting for the buybacks to begin,” Spatacco summed up.

Spatacco’s bullish outlook is very much in line with Wall Street, where analysts remain bullish about Micron’s prospects. data.title: ‘The Time Has Come,’ Says Top Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab’s (NASDAQ:RKLB) customers and its shareholders seem to be reading different stories. Satellite operators are lining up to fly on Neutron, the company’s new medium-lift rocket, and they’re paying more for a spot even though it has yet to launch.

Meanwhile, investors have been heading for the exits since late spring. The selloff deepened after SpaceX’s June IPO, and a steady stream of new Rocket Lab shares hasn’t helped. Then came a setback on Neutron itself. The rocket is central to Rocket Lab’s future, since it can carry far bigger payloads than the small Electron rocket the company flies today, and it’s key to the company’s path to profitability. Its first flight was supposed to happen before the end of this year, but it has now been pushed into 2027 after engineers found flaws in a fuel tank dome.

With all that as backdrop, the shares now trade more than 60% below their late-May record.

This is often when bulls will tell you it’s time to load up, and that is exactly what investor James Foord, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, thinks you should do. Foord believes the space company’s third-quarter report deserves another look.

Foord’s first point is that the bottom line makes the quarter look worse than it was. Rocket Lab posted a net loss of $79.7 million, or $0.12 per share, far wider than the $0.02 loss Wall Street expected. A large part of it came from one-off charges tied to the Iridium deal. That includes a $27.3 million write-off after Rocket Lab canceled a $3.6 billion bridge loan it never used. Underneath that, revenue jumped 73% year over year to $267.8 million, beating management’s own forecast. Non-GAAP gross margin of 38.4% also came in above guidance, and operating cash flow turned positive at $7.2 million.

The order book is what really stands out for the 5-star investor. Backlog grew 52% from the prior quarter to $3.57 billion. More than $515 million of that came from eight Neutron missions signed in Q3, which brings the rocket’s total to 16 booked flights. Anyone signing up now is looking at a slot in the 2030s. Rocket Lab also raised Neutron’s base price to $70 million for several of the new contracts, up from $55 million. CFO Adam Spice said the company passed on some extra bookings to hold out for better prices. Foord notes that the delay hasn’t cost Rocket Lab any customers, at least none that are known.

There may be no more share sales, either. Rocket Lab has the money lined up for the ~$8 billion Iridium purchase, and management expects adjusted EBITDA to turn positive within six months of Neutron’s first successful flight. If that holds, the investor sees little need for more fundraising.

The stock isn’t cheap, and Foord doesn’t pretend otherwise. Its enterprise value is roughly 40 times trailing 12-month sales. Still, management said about a third of the backlog should become revenue over the next 12 months, which helps put 2027 revenue at about $1.4 billion on the investor’s estimates, or roughly 43% growth. A clean Neutron launch could also justify a somewhat richer multiple.

Neutron still carries real risk. Another delay or a failed debut would hurt, and the Iridium deal still needs FCC approval. Those, however, don’t dull the bull case.

“All in all,” Foord summed up, “I think the worst is behind Rocket Lab. The Neutron delay is known, the dilution is done, and the business just posted its best quarter ever. The stock won’t go up in a straight line, and I’d leave some room to add on a dip. But for investors who have been waiting for an entry, I believe this is it.”

To this end, Foord rates RKLB stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Foord’s track record, click here)

The analyst consensus has reached the same conclusion, one based on 15 Buys and 3 Holds. The forecast calls for one-year returns of 71%, considering the average price target lands at $95.41. (See RKLB stock forecast)

Among the many dividend ETFs available, Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD), Vanguard International High Dividend Yield ETF (VYMI), and Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG) stand out for different reasons. Using the TipRanks’ ETF Comparison Tool, we compared VYMI, SCHD, and VIG to find out which one may be the best fit for investors seeking dividend income.

Each ETF can play a different role in an income portfolio. SCHD focuses on U.S. dividend stocks, VYMI adds international exposure, and VIG targets companies with a strong record of dividend growth.

Key Comparison

Vanguard International High Dividend Yield ETF (VYMI)

VYMI provides exposure to high-dividend-paying stocks outside the U.S. It tracks the FTSE All-World ex US High Dividend Yield Index. VYMI pays a quarterly dividend of $0.82 per share. Currently, the ETF holds 1,482 stocks with total assets worth $21.89 billion. Its top holdings are Roche Holdings (RHHBY), Shell (SHEL), and Novartis (NVS).

VYMI may appeal to investors who want exposure to international markets, which many U.S.-focused portfolios lack. U.S. stocks have often traded at higher valuations and offered lower dividend yields than international stocks.

But international stocks also carry currency risk and can face greater volatility due to geopolitical events. Foreign companies may also change their dividend payouts more often than U.S. companies.

Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD)

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD) currently offers a dividend yield of 3% and pays a quarterly dividend of $0.27 per share. The fund owns 100 stocks and manages $123.77 billion in assets. Its top three holdings are Texas Instruments (TXN), Procter & Gamble (PG), and Coca-Cola Company (KO).

SCHD provides regular income and has a history of growing its dividend. Among the risks, SCHD has limited exposure to major tech stocks and leans more toward traditional value sectors. This could limit its gains when tech stocks lead the market.

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG)

The Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG) invests in U.S. companies with a strong track record of raising their dividends. VIG tracks the S&P U.S. Dividend Growers Index. VIG currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.93 per share, giving it a 1.46% yield. The ETF holds 334 stocks and manages about $117.94 billion in assets. Its top holdings include Apple (AAPL), Eli Lilly (LLY), and Microsoft (MSFT).

VIG only includes companies that have raised their dividends for at least 10 straight years. It also avoids stocks with very high yields, which may have less sustainable dividend payouts. However, with a yield below 2%, VIG may not suit investors who want higher income today.

Conclusion

SCHD stands out for investors who want higher income today, while VIG is better suited to long-term dividend growth and wealth building. VYMI adds international exposure.

data.title: IREN Stock Has Plunged 43% in a Month — But Don’t Panic, Says Top Investor
data.description:
IREN (NASDAQ:IREN) stock is falling another 4% in Tuesday’s trading session, extending a brutal selloff that has erased 43% of its value over the past month. The longer-term picture looks even worse, with shares now down 67% over the past 12 months. Once a market favorite for its transformation from Bitcoin mining into AI cloud infrastructure, IREN is struggling to convince investors that its expansion plans will deliver the financial rewards they anticipated.

IREN recently postponed its target for exceeding $4 billion in annualized run-rate revenue until early 2027, following customer-requested design changes and supplier-related delays. Meanwhile, another $6 billion in funding remains necessary to support broader expansion plans through fiscal 2027, raising fears of additional borrowing or equity dilution.

Yet, top investor Yiannis Zourmpanos, who ranks among the top 1% of stock pros on TipRanks, believes the market has become far too pessimistic about IREN’s prospects. Rather than joining the rush for the exits, Zourmpanos has taken advantage of the recent collapse to establish a position.

“I initiated a long position in IREN since the pullback has materially improved the risk/reward with limited downside,” the investor explained.

Zourmpanos believes IREN’s improving commercial performance provides reason for confidence. Quarterly AI Cloud sales nearly tripled to $200 million, while the revenue backlog reached $20.3 billion, providing greater visibility into the company’s future revenue potential.

Zourmpanos also considers IREN’s ownership of $6 billion in data center assets an important competitive advantage over operators relying on leased facilities. Such properties provide valuable collateral for obtaining financing, although constructing these sites requires considerable upfront spending before cash begins arriving.

However, the investor recognizes that several obstacles could prevent IREN from achieving its financial targets within the expected timeframe. Only a fraction of secured electricity capacity currently supports operational computing facilities, leaving extensive construction, equipment installation, and customer approval work unfinished. Additional financing could also become more expensive if lenders tighten their requirements, potentially forcing further stock issuance.

Nevertheless, Zourmpanos believes investors have become overly focused on those hazards while overlooking the company’s longer-term possibilities.

“I think that current correction factors are significant execution risks while ignoring growth potential,” Zourmpanos argued.

His valuation comparisons illustrate why the recent collapse has changed his perspective on IREN’s investment appeal. Shares currently trade at nearly six times estimated fiscal 2027 revenue on an enterprise-value basis, versus 13.4 for Nebius and 6.9 for CoreWeave. That discount, according to Zourmpanos, suggests considerable room for appreciation if planned deployments proceed successfully and contracted customers begin generating expected payments.

Looking further ahead, consensus forecasts anticipate annual revenue reaching $2.39 billion in fiscal 2027 before climbing to $7.33 billion the following year. Although those projections depend on successful execution, they illustrate the scale of potential revenue growth as additional computing resources become operational.

Ultimately, Zourmpanos sees the recent collapse as an opportunity for investors willing to tolerate uncertainty while awaiting IREN’s next growth phase, rating the stock a Strong Buy. (See Zourmpanos’ track record, click here)

While Zourmpanos has gone all-in with his Strong Buy rating, Wall Street is taking a somewhat more measured approach. IREN currently commands a Moderate Buy consensus, with 8 analysts recommending Buy, and 3 staying on the sidelines. Nevertheless, the average price target of $56.50 suggests shares could surge 257% over the coming year. (See IREN stock forecast)

data.title: 3 Vanguard ETFs Loaded with Nvidia Stock (NVDA) That Offer 30%+ Upside
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) will report its fiscal Q3 results today after the market closes. Analysts expect EPS to rise about 90% to $2.48, while revenue is forecast to jump nearly 91% year-over-year to $108.96 billion. Using the Best Vanguard ETFs tool, we identified three funds with significant Nvidia exposure: Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT), Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF (VOOG), and Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF (MGK).

TipRanks’ ETF Analyst Consensus, which combines analyst ratings for each fund’s holdings, gives MGK and VOOG Strong Buy ratings and VGT a Moderate Buy rating.

Among the three, VGT has an average price target of $152.24, suggesting 44% upside. MGK has an average price target of $109.93, pointing to 33% upside. Meanwhile, VOOG has a price target of $105.80, implying 38% upside.

Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT)

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF is focused solely on U.S. technology stocks. Nvidia stock makes up 17% of the fund’s portfolio. Other major holdings include Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Broadcom (AVGO), and Micron (MU).

Overall, VGT has 316 stocks with assets worth $141.61 billion.

VGT has a beta of 1.51, meaning it tends to move more than the overall market. It also has an expense ratio of 0.09%.

Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF (VOOG)

The Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF tracks the growth segment of the S&P 500, focusing on large-cap companies with strong earnings momentum. Its biggest holding is NVDA at 14.20% of the portfolio, followed by MSFT and AAPL.

Overall, VOOG holds 154 stocks and manages approximately $26.61 billion in assets. The fund has a beta of 1.27.

Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF (MGK)

Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF focuses on the largest U.S. growth companies, mainly big technology and consumer brands with strong growth potential. The fund has a beta of 1.31.

MGK’s biggest holding is NVDA at 13.11%. Other major stocks include AAPL, MSFT, Meta (META), Alphabet (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN).

Overall, MGK holds 53 stocks and manages about $32.96 billion in assets. The ETF also offers a low expense ratio of 0.05%.

data.title: ‘Get Ready for Next Year,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Aaaand down it goes again. Micron (NASDAQ:MU) looked set for a breather from the recent relentless selling on Tuesday morning. Memory names were bouncing before the bell as South Korean chip stocks recovered and bargain hunters moved in.

No dice. The bounce faded soon after the open, with the market still working through Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, new U.S. export rules on AI chips, and a class action lawsuit accusing the big memory makers of colluding on DRAM prices. Nvidia, a major buyer of Micron’s high-bandwidth memory, reports after the close tonight, and the whole AI trade is waiting on that result.

Meanwhile, given the stock’s brutal selloff, the shares are now changing hands 43% below their late-June peak.

But for investors losing hope that this former high-flyer will ever recover, investor Rick Orford, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, is looking past the current bloodbath and focusing on 2027. And, according to Orford, that could be a very good thing for Micron investors.

Orford’s case starts with Micron’s role in the AI build-out. The company makes the DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that AI servers depend on. Its cloud and data center business powered fiscal 2026, helped by both strong demand and higher prices. Management says AI is using up memory faster than the industry can add capacity, so Micron has shifted its mix toward premium data center products. The most powerful AI processors need large amounts of HBM to keep data moving, and hyperscaler budgets are paying for it. Micron has also added new server memory, SSDs built for AI workloads, and chips aimed at physical AI.

For the investor, that shortage is the heart of the story. A leading-edge fab takes years and huge amounts of capital to bring online, which keeps supply tight and supports pricing and margins across the business. Micron’s own expansion shows how long it takes. Its first new Idaho fab isn’t expected to start DRAM wafer output until next year, and the New York project will add supply over the next two decades. In September, management said it expects supply-demand conditions to be much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than they were in fiscal 2026.

Orford also notes that Micron’s AI exposure isn’t speculative. Demand from customers and limits on supply can be seen right now. And as the only memory chipmaker of its size based in the U.S., Micron has an edge as governments and tech companies push to move production closer to home.

The 5-star investor doesn’t play down the risks. Memory is still a cyclical business. If AI spending cools or producers overbuild, prices could fall. There’s also the question of whether hyperscalers will earn enough on their AI spending to keep building data centers, and a slowdown there would hurt Micron’s outlook.

Even so, Orford thinks the share price already reflects plenty of caution. Micron trades at a forward P/E of about 4.2, a low multiple for a company this central to the AI build-out. “Looking ahead,” Orford summed up, “with memory becoming increasingly vital to the AI build-out and Micron strengthening its market position, the company could surprise investors as one of 2027’s biggest AI stock winners.” (To watch Orford’s track record, click here)

Almost all of the Street’s analysts concur. Based on 28 Buys vs. 1 Hold, the consensus view is that this stock is a Strong Buy. Over the next year, shares are expected to climb 137% higher, given the average target clocks in at $1,624. (See Micron stock forecast)
